definition: Inson tanasiga tayanch beruvchi, ichki a'zolarni himoyalovchi va harakatni ta'minlovchi 206 ta suyak va bo'g'imlar majmuasi. (Jami 61 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Tana harakati, qomatni saqlash va issiqlik ajratishni ta'minlovchi 600 dan ortiq skelet mushaklari majmuasi. (Jami 55 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Yurak va qon tomirlari (arteriya, vena, kapillarlar) orqali butun tanaga qon, kislorod va ozuqa moddalarini yetkazib beruvchi tizim. (Jami 60 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Bosh miya, orqa miya va asab tolalari orqali butun organizm faoliyatini va barcha sezgilarni boshqaruvchi bosh markaziy tizim. (Jami 708 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Burun bo'shlig'i, kekirdak, bronxlar va o'pka orqali havoni qabul qilib, qonni kislorod bilan to'yintiruvchi va karbonat angidridni chiqaruvchi tizim. (Jami 246 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Og'iz bo'shlig'idan to to'g'ri ichakkacha bo'lgan, oziq-ovqatni qayta ishlab organizmga kerakli moddalarni so'ruvchi hazm a'zolari tizimi. (Jami 162 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Qalqonsimon bez, gipofiz, buyrak usti bezi kabi a'zolar orqali qonga gormonlar ajratib, tana funksiyalarini boshqaruvchi bezlar tizimi. (Jami 70 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Organizmning infeksiyalar, viruslar va bakteriyalarga qarshi kurashuvchi mudofaa qalqoni (limfa tugunlari, taloq, timus). (Jami 42 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Buyraklar, siydik yo'llari va qovuq orqali qonni zararli moddalardan tozalab, ortiqcha suv va tuzlarni chiqaruvchi a'zolar tizimi. (Jami 40 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Nasl qoldirish, jinsiy gormonlar va hujayralarni ishlab chiqarish uchun mas'ul a'zolar tizimi. (Jami 32 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).
Tananing eng katta a'zolar tizimi: teri, soch, tirnoqlar va teri bezlaridan iborat bo'lib, tanani tashqi muhitdan himoya qiladi. (Jami 72 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).

uzbek: Maxsus sezgi a'zolari tizimi (Special Senses system)
definition: Ko'rish (ko'z), eshitish va muvozanat (quloq), hid bilish, ta'm bilish a'zolarini o'z ichiga oluvchi sezgi tizimi. (Jami 5 ta anatomik tuzilmani birlashtiradi).

Inson tanasi sohasi: Bosh sohasi. The uppermost part of the body containing the brain, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth. The skull (cranium) protects the brain, while the face contains the primary sensory organs.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Yuz sohasi. The anterior part of the head from the forehead to the chin. Contains muscles of facial expression, the orbits housing the eyes, the nasal cavity, oral cavity, and associated structures.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Bo'yin sohasi. The region connecting the head to the trunk. Contains the cervical vertebrae, major blood vessels (carotid arteries, jugular veins), the larynx, pharynx, trachea, esophagus, thyroid gland, and numerous muscles and nerves.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Ko'krak qafasi sohasi. The chest region bounded by the rib cage. Contains the lungs, heart, great vessels, esophagus, trachea, and thoracic duct. The thoracic cage provides protection for vital organs while allowing respiratory movements.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Qorin sohasi. The region between the thorax and pelvis containing the majority of digestive organs including the stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys. The abdominal wall consists of layered muscles providing support and movement.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Chanoq sohasi. The lower trunk region formed by the pelvic girdle. Contains the urinary bladder, rectum, and reproductive organs. The bony pelvis supports the weight of the upper body and provides attachment for lower limb muscles.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Orqa / Bel sohasi. The posterior aspect of the trunk from the neck to the pelvis. Contains the vertebral column (spine), spinal cord, and layers of muscles responsible for posture, trunk movement, and protection of the spinal cord.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Yelka sohasi. The region between the shoulder and elbow containing the humerus bone. Major muscles include the biceps brachii (flexion) and triceps brachii (extension). The brachial artery and major nerves traverse this region.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Bilak sohasi. The region between the elbow and wrist containing the radius and ulna bones. Houses the flexor and extensor muscle groups that control hand and wrist movements, as well as the radial and ulnar arteries.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Qo'l panjasi sohasi. The terminal part of the upper limb consisting of the carpals (wrist bones), metacarpals, and phalanges (finger bones). Contains intrinsic muscles, tendons, and an extensive nerve supply enabling fine motor control and tactile sensation.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Son sohasi. The region between the hip and knee containing the femur, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Major muscle groups include the quadriceps (extension), hamstrings (flexion), and adductors. The femoral artery provides major blood supply.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Boldir sohasi. The region between the knee and ankle containing the tibia and fibula bones. The anterior and posterior compartments house muscles controlling ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, as well as the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Oyoq panjasi sohasi. The terminal part of the lower limb consisting of the tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges. The foot contains arches (medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, transverse) that distribute body weight and absorb shock during locomotion.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Yelka bo'g'imi sohasi. The junction between the upper limb and trunk. The shoulder girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula, with the glenohumeral joint being the most mobile joint in the body. The rotator cuff muscles stabilize the joint.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Chanoq-son sohasi. The junction between the lower limb and trunk. The hip joint (coxal joint) is a ball-and-socket joint formed by the femoral head and acetabulum of the pelvis. Surrounded by powerful muscles, it provides stability for weight-bearing and locomotion.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Umurtqa pog'onasi sohasi. The vertebral column consisting of 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral fused, 4 coccygeal fused). It protects the spinal cord, supports the head and trunk, and allows flexible movement. Intervertebral discs provide cushioning between vertebrae.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Bosh miya sohasi. The primary organ of the central nervous system enclosed within the cranium. Consists of the cerebrum (cerebral cortex and white matter), cerebellum, brainstem, and diencephalon. The brain processes sensory information, controls motor function, and is the seat of consciousness, cognition, and emotion.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Yurak sohasi (Mediastinum). The mediastinal region centered on the heart and great vessels. The heart occupies the middle mediastinum and is enclosed in the pericardium. Major structures include the ascending aorta, superior vena cava, pulmonary trunk, and pulmonary veins.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Ko'z sohasi (Orbita). The orbital region containing the eyeball and its accessory structures. The eye converts light into neural signals for visual perception. Structures include the cornea, lens, retina, iris, and optic nerve, along with extraocular muscles, eyelids, and the lacrimal apparatus.

Inson tanasi sohasi: Quloq sohasi. The region containing the external, middle, and inner ear structures. The ear converts sound waves into neural signals for auditory perception and contains the vestibular apparatus for balance. Key structures include the tympanic membrane, ossicles, cochlea, and semicircular canals.
Anatomik ta'rif: Conducting impulses or fluids toward a central point. Afferent nerve fibers carry sensory signals toward the central nervous system; afferent vessels carry blood toward an organ.

Anatomik ta'rif: The standard reference posture used in anatomy: body erect, face forward, feet together, arms at the sides with palms facing anteriorly. All anatomical terms of direction are defined relative to this position.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated toward the front of the body. In anatomical position, the anterior surface faces forward. Synonymous with ventral in standard anatomical position.
Anatomik ta'rif: On the opposite side of the body. Most descending motor and ascending pain pathways decussate (cross), so lesions produce contralateral deficits.
Anatomik ta'rif: A vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior portions, also called the frontal plane. It passes perpendicular to the sagittal plane.
Anatomik ta'rif: Located further from the body surface, beneath more superficial structures. Deep muscles lie beneath superficial muscles and closer to bone.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated further from the point of origin or attachment, typically the trunk. Used primarily for limb structures where distal means further from the body's midline.
Anatomik ta'rif: Pertaining to the back surface of the body; synonymous with posterior in humans. Dorsal also describes the top surface of the foot (dorsum pedis) and hand (dorsum manus).

Anatomik ta'rif: Conducting impulses or fluids away from a central point. Efferent nerve fibers carry motor signals away from the CNS to muscles and glands; efferent vessels carry blood away from an organ.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated below or toward the foot end of the body (also called caudal). The kidneys are inferior to the diaphragm.
Anatomik ta'rif: On the same side of the body. Ipsilateral motor and sensory pathways travel on the same side without crossing; the term is clinically important in neurological localization.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated further from the median plane (midline) of the body. The fibula is lateral to the tibia in the leg.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated closer to the median plane (midline) of the body. The ulna is medial to the radius in the forearm.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated toward the back of the body. In anatomical position, the posterior surface faces backward. Synonymous with dorsal in standard anatomical position.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated closer to the point of origin or attachment, typically the trunk. Used primarily for limb structures where proximal means closer to the body's midline.

Anatomik ta'rif: A vertical plane that divides the body into left and right portions. The midsagittal (median) plane passes through the midline; parasagittal planes are parallel but offset from the midline.
Anatomik ta'rif: Located closer to the body surface. Superficial structures are closer to the skin than deep structures of the same region.
Anatomik ta'rif: Situated above or toward the head end of the body (also called cranial). The heart is superior to the diaphragm.

Anatomik ta'rif: A horizontal plane that divides the body into superior and inferior portions, also called the axial or cross-sectional plane. CT and MRI images are commonly displayed in this orientation.
Anatomik ta'rif: Pertaining to the belly or front surface of the body; synonymous with anterior in humans. In four-legged animals, ventral refers to the underside of the body.
Anatomik ta'rif: The tough outer fibrocartilaginous ring of an intervertebral disc that surrounds and contains the gelatinous nucleus pulposus. Tears in the annulus fibrosus allow disc herniation.
Anatomik ta'rif: A joint or point of contact between two or more bones. Articulations are classified as fibrous (immovable), cartilaginous (slightly movable), or synovial (freely movable).

Anatomik ta'rif: A fluid-filled sac lined with synovial membrane that reduces friction between tendons, muscles, and bony prominences. Inflammation of a bursa (bursitis) is a common cause of joint pain.

Anatomik ta'rif: The site where a tendon, ligament, or joint capsule attaches to bone. Enthesopathy (inflammation at entheses) is a hallmark of seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis.

Anatomik ta'rif: A sheet or band of fibrous connective tissue that envelops, separates, and supports muscles and organs. Deep fascia compartmentalizes muscle groups; superficial fascia lies beneath the skin.
Anatomik ta'rif: The distal, usually more movable attachment point of a skeletal muscle. During contraction, the insertion is drawn toward the origin to produce movement.

Anatomik ta'rif: A sheet of deep fascia extending inward from the outer investing fascia to attach to bone, separating adjacent muscle compartments. Injury or swelling within a compartment can raise pressure and cause compartment syndrome.

Anatomik ta'rif: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between adjacent vertebral bodies consisting of an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner nucleus pulposus. Discs account for roughly 25% of total spine height and allow spinal flexibility.
Anatomik ta'rif: The outermost layer of deep fascia that encircles an entire limb or body region, encasing all structures within it. In the lower limb, the investing fascia is called the fascia lata.

Anatomik ta'rif: A ring of fibrocartilage attached to the rim of certain joint sockets (particularly the hip and shoulder glenoid) that deepens the articular cavity and improves joint stability. Labral tears are a common sports injury.
Anatomik ta'rif: A band of dense fibrous connective tissue that connects bone to bone, providing stability to joints. Ligaments limit excessive movement and prevent dislocation.

Anatomik ta'rif: A crescent-shaped fibrocartilage pad found in certain joints, most notably the knee. Menisci improve joint congruence, distribute load across the articular surface, and aid in shock absorption.

Anatomik ta'rif: The interface where muscle fibers meet tendon, representing the transition zone between contractile and non-contractile tissue. This region is a common site of muscle strains during eccentric loading.
Anatomik ta'rif: The gelatinous, water-rich core of an intervertebral disc that acts as a shock absorber and distributes compressive forces. It is a remnant of the embryonic notochord.
Anatomik ta'rif: The proximal, usually less movable attachment point of a skeletal muscle. During contraction, the origin remains relatively fixed while the insertion moves toward it.

Anatomik ta'rif: A seam or ridge of tissue formed where two symmetrical halves meet, often serving as a tendinous intersection or midline union. The pterygomandibular raphe is a clinically important landmark in dental anesthesia.

Anatomik ta'rif: A small bone embedded within a tendon, typically near a joint, that protects the tendon and improves its mechanical advantage. The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body.

Anatomik ta'rif: A viscous, egg-white-like fluid secreted by the synovial membrane that lubricates synovial joints and provides nutrients to avascular articular cartilage. Its viscosity is due to hyaluronic acid.

Anatomik ta'rif: The inner lining of a joint capsule that secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish articular cartilage. Inflammation of the synovial membrane (synovitis) is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis.
Anatomik ta'rif: A fibrous band of connective tissue that attaches a muscle to a bone. Tendons transmit the force of muscle contraction to produce movement at joints.

Anatomik ta'rif: A connection between two blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, or other tubular structures. Arterial anastomoses provide collateral circulation to maintain blood supply if one vessel is occluded.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cluster of specialized conduction cells at the base of the right atrium near the interventricular septum that delays electrical transmission between the atria and ventricles, allowing atrial contraction to complete before ventricular contraction begins.

Anatomik ta'rif: One of the two superior receiving chambers of the heart. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation via the vena cavae; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs via the pulmonary veins.

Anatomik ta'rif: A collection of heart muscle cells (specialized cardiac fibers) that transmit electrical impulses from the atrioventricular node to the right and left bundle branches and then to the Purkinje fibers. Also called the atrioventricular bundle.
Anatomik ta'rif: The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart chambers relax and fill with blood. Ventricular diastole allows the ventricles to receive blood from the atria.

Anatomik ta'rif: The thin inner lining of the heart chambers and cardiac valves, continuous with the endothelium of blood vessels. Endocarditis is a serious infection of this layer, particularly affecting valves.

Anatomik ta'rif: The single layer of squamous epithelial cells lining the interior surface of blood vessels and lymphatic vessels. The endothelium regulates vascular tone, coagulation, and inflammation.
Anatomik ta'rif: The interior space of a tubular structure, such as a blood vessel or intestine. The diameter of the vascular lumen determines blood flow and resistance.

Anatomik ta'rif: The muscular middle layer of the heart wall, composed of specialized cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes). It constitutes the bulk of the heart and is responsible for the pumping action.
Anatomik ta'rif: The passage of blood through the vascular bed of a tissue or organ. Adequate perfusion is essential for oxygen and nutrient delivery and waste removal.

Anatomik ta'rif: The double-layered fibroserous sac enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels. The fibrous pericardium limits over-distension; the serous pericardium secretes pericardial fluid to reduce friction.

Anatomik ta'rif: Specialized cardiac muscle fibers in the subendocardial layer that rapidly conduct electrical impulses from the bundle branches to the ventricular myocardium, ensuring synchronous ventricular contraction.

Anatomik ta'rif: The muscular wall dividing the heart into left and right halves. The interventricular septum separates the two ventricles; the interatrial septum separates the two atria. Septal defects are common congenital heart anomalies.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cluster of pacemaker cells in the right atrial wall near the opening of the superior vena cava that spontaneously generates electrical impulses, setting the intrinsic heart rate. Also called the SA node or cardiac pacemaker.
Anatomik ta'rif: The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart chambers contract and pump blood. Ventricular systole ejects blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

Anatomik ta'rif: The outermost layer of a blood vessel wall, composed of fibrous connective tissue that anchors the vessel to surrounding structures. It contains the vasa vasorum (tiny vessels supplying the vessel wall) and autonomic nerve fibers.

Anatomik ta'rif: The innermost layer of a blood vessel wall, consisting of endothelium resting on a thin basement membrane and a subendothelial connective tissue layer. Atherosclerotic plaques develop within the tunica intima.
Anatomik ta'rif: The middle layer of a blood vessel wall, composed of smooth muscle and elastic tissue. It is the thickest layer in arteries and controls vessel diameter and hence blood pressure.

Anatomik ta'rif: A structure that ensures unidirectional blood flow through the heart. The four cardiac valves are the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral (bicuspid), and aortic valves; they open and close passively in response to pressure gradients.

Anatomik ta'rif: One of the two inferior pumping chambers of the heart. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation.

Anatomik ta'rif: Star-shaped glial cells that are the most abundant cells in the brain. Astrocytes maintain the blood-brain barrier, regulate extracellular ion concentrations, provide metabolic support to neurons, and participate in synaptic modulation.

Anatomik ta'rif: The long, slender projection of a neuron that conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons or effector organs. Axons may be myelinated or unmyelinated and can extend over a meter in length.

Anatomik ta'rif: A selective permeability barrier formed by tight junctions between cerebral endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte foot processes, that tightly regulates the passage of substances from blood into brain tissue. It protects the CNS from pathogens and toxins but also limits drug delivery.

Anatomik ta'rif: The region connecting the cerebrum and cerebellum to the spinal cord, consisting of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. It contains vital autonomic centers for respiration, cardiovascular regulation, and the nuclei of most cranial nerves.

Anatomik ta'rif: The large hindbrain structure posterior to the brainstem that coordinates voluntary movement, balance, and motor learning. Cerebellar damage produces ataxia (incoordination) and dysmetria (inability to judge distances).

Anatomik ta'rif: The outer layer of gray matter covering the cerebral hemispheres, organized into six cellular layers (laminae). It is responsible for higher cognitive functions including consciousness, sensory perception, language, and voluntary motor control.

Anatomik ta'rif: Branching cytoplasmic extensions of a neuron that receive synaptic inputs from other neurons and conduct electrical signals toward the cell body. Most neurons have multiple dendrites, greatly increasing their surface area for synaptic contact.
Anatomik ta'rif: An area of skin supplied by sensory nerve fibers from a single spinal nerve root. Dermatome maps are used clinically to localize spinal cord and nerve root lesions.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cluster of neuron cell bodies located outside the central nervous system. Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies; autonomic ganglia contain postganglionic neuron cell bodies.

Anatomik ta'rif: Non-neuronal supporting cells of the nervous system that provide structural support, insulation, nutrients, and immune defense. Glia outnumber neurons in the brain and include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells.

Anatomik ta'rif: A small region at the base of the diencephalon that controls the autonomic nervous system, regulates pituitary hormone secretion, and maintains homeostasis of body temperature, hunger, thirst, and circadian rhythms.

Anatomik ta'rif: The three protective membranes (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater) surrounding the brain and spinal cord. They contain cerebrospinal fluid and protect the central nervous system.

Anatomik ta'rif: A fatty insulating sheath surrounding many nerve fibers that increases the speed of electrical impulse conduction. Produced by Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

Anatomik ta'rif: The fundamental excitable cell of the nervous system, specialized for receiving and transmitting electrical and chemical signals. A neuron consists of a cell body (soma), dendrites, and an axon.

Anatomik ta'rif: Glial cells of the central nervous system that produce myelin sheaths around axons, enabling rapid saltatory conduction. A single oligodendrocyte can myelinate up to 50 axon segments; their destruction underlies demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis.
Anatomik ta'rif: A network of intersecting nerves or blood vessels. Major nerve plexuses include the cervical, brachial, lumbar, and sacral plexuses that supply the limbs and body wall.

Anatomik ta'rif: Glial cells of the peripheral nervous system that form myelin sheaths around axons. Unlike oligodendrocytes, each Schwann cell myelinates only one axon segment; they also facilitate peripheral nerve regeneration after injury.

Anatomik ta'rif: The cylindrical bundle of neural tissue extending from the medulla oblongata to the conus medullaris (approximately L1-L2 vertebral level). It contains ascending sensory tracts and descending motor tracts, and mediates spinal reflexes.
Anatomik ta'rif: The junction between two neurons or between a neuron and an effector cell. Neurotransmitters released at synapses transmit signals across the synaptic cleft.

Anatomik ta'rif: A paired gray-matter structure in the diencephalon that serves as the major relay station for sensory and motor signals to and from the cerebral cortex. Nearly all sensory information (except olfaction) is processed through the thalamus.

Anatomik ta'rif: A localized collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue, resulting from bacterial infection. Abscesses require drainage (surgical or spontaneous) to resolve; antibiotics alone are generally insufficient.

Anatomik ta'rif: Abnormal fibrous bands that form between tissue surfaces following inflammation, injury, or surgery. Intra-abdominal adhesions are a leading cause of small bowel obstruction and pelvic pain.

Anatomik ta'rif: Decrease in the size of a tissue or organ due to loss of cells or reduction in cell size. Atrophy can result from disuse, denervation, inadequate nutrition, or loss of hormonal stimulation.

Anatomik ta'rif: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in interstitial tissue spaces, causing swelling. Edema can result from increased capillary pressure, decreased plasma proteins, lymphatic obstruction, or increased capillary permeability.

Anatomik ta'rif: Obstruction of a blood vessel by a mass (embolus) that has traveled from another site in the circulation. Common emboli include blood clots (thromboembolism), fat globules, air bubbles, and amniotic fluid.

Anatomik ta'rif: An abnormal communication between two epithelium-lined surfaces, such as two organs or between an organ and the skin. Fistulae may arise from infection, inflammation (e.g., Crohn's disease), or trauma and often require surgical repair.

Anatomik ta'rif: Escape of blood from a ruptured blood vessel. Hemorrhage can be classified by location (e.g., intracranial, subarachnoid, gastrointestinal) and is life-threatening when significant volumes are lost rapidly.

Anatomik ta'rif: Protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening in its containing wall. Intervertebral disc herniation occurs when the nucleus pulposus protrudes through a torn annulus fibrosus, often compressing nearby nerve roots.

Anatomik ta'rif: Increase in the size of a tissue or organ due to enlargement of its constituent cells. Cardiac hypertrophy occurs in response to chronic pressure overload; skeletal muscle hypertrophy results from exercise.

Anatomik ta'rif: Tissue necrosis resulting from prolonged ischemia due to obstruction of arterial supply or venous drainage. Myocardial infarction (heart attack) and cerebral infarction (ischemic stroke) are the most clinically significant examples.

Anatomik ta'rif: A protective vascular and cellular response to injury, infection, or irritation characterized by the cardinal signs: redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor), and loss of function (functio laesa). It can be acute or chronic.
Anatomik ta'rif: Insufficient blood supply to a tissue or organ, resulting in oxygen deprivation and potential tissue damage. Prolonged ischemia leads to infarction (tissue death).

Anatomik ta'rif: Relating to or caused by ischemia (insufficient blood supply). The adjective is used in clinical terms such as ischemic heart disease, ischemic stroke, and ischemic colitis to indicate vascular insufficiency as the underlying mechanism.

Anatomik ta'rif: The spread of malignant cells from a primary tumor to distant sites via blood vessels, lymphatics, or body cavities, where they form secondary tumors. Metastasis is the primary cause of cancer-related mortality.
Anatomik ta'rif: Death of cells or tissues due to injury, disease, or failure of blood supply. Unlike apoptosis (programmed cell death), necrosis is a pathological process that triggers inflammation.

Anatomik ta'rif: An abnormal mass of tissue resulting from uncontrolled cell proliferation. Neoplasms are classified as benign (non-invasive) or malignant (invasive, capable of metastasis); the term is synonymous with 'tumor' in common clinical usage.

Anatomik ta'rif: Downward displacement or falling of an organ from its normal position. Mitral valve prolapse, uterine prolapse, and rectal prolapse are common clinical examples, each with distinct anatomical and functional consequences.

Anatomik ta'rif: A life-threatening systemic inflammatory response to infection in which the body's immune response causes widespread tissue damage. Septic shock is the most severe form, characterized by refractory hypotension and multi-organ failure.
Anatomik ta'rif: Abnormal narrowing of a passage or opening in the body. Vascular stenosis (such as carotid or coronary) restricts blood flow and can cause ischemia.

Anatomik ta'rif: The formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within a blood vessel, obstructing normal blood flow. Thrombosis can occur in arteries (arterial thrombosis) or veins (venous thrombosis, commonly deep vein thrombosis/DVT).

Anatomik ta'rif: A rounded, knuckle-like articular prominence on a bone. Condyles form part of synovial joint surfaces; examples include the medial and lateral condyles of the femur and the mandibular condyle of the temporomandibular joint.

Anatomik ta'rif: A narrow ridge or raised border along a bone surface. The iliac crest of the pelvis, the tibial crest (shin), and the intertrochanteric crest of the femur are clinically important surface landmarks.

Anatomik ta'rif: The shaft or central portion of a long bone, composed primarily of compact cortical bone surrounding a medullary cavity filled with yellow (fat) marrow in adults. It provides rigidity and longitudinal strength.

Anatomik ta'rif: A thin vascular membrane lining the inner surface of bone (medullary cavity) and the surfaces of the Haversian canals. It contains osteoblasts and osteoclasts involved in bone remodeling.

Anatomik ta'rif: A projection on the surface of a condyle that serves primarily as a site of muscle and ligament attachment rather than articulation. The medial epicondyle of the humerus is a common site of injury (golfer's elbow); the lateral epicondyle is affected in tennis elbow.

Anatomik ta'rif: The rounded end of a long bone, composed mainly of cancellous (spongy) bone and covered with articular cartilage. The epiphyses develop from secondary ossification centers and are separated from the diaphysis by the epiphyseal plate in growing bone.

Anatomik ta'rif: A small, flat articular surface on a bone. Vertebral facet joints (zygapophyseal joints) allow gliding movements between adjacent vertebrae; costal facets on thoracic vertebrae articulate with the ribs.

Anatomik ta'rif: A membranous gap between the incompletely ossified skull bones of a newborn, allowing the cranium to deform during birth and the brain to grow postnatally. The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is the largest and typically closes by 18-24 months of age.

Anatomik ta'rif: A natural opening or passage in a bone or other anatomical structure through which nerves, blood vessels, or other structures pass. Examples include the foramen magnum (allowing the brainstem to pass through the skull) and the obturator foramen of the pelvis.

Anatomik ta'rif: A shallow concave depression on the surface of a bone, often serving as an articular surface or as attachment for muscles. Examples include the glenoid fossa of the scapula (shoulder joint socket) and the olecranon fossa of the humerus.

Anatomik ta'rif: The structural unit of compact cortical bone, also called an osteon, consisting of concentric lamellae of bone matrix surrounding a central Haversian canal that contains blood vessels and nerves. Multiple osteons give compact bone its characteristic appearance in cross-section.

Anatomik ta'rif: The region between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone that contains the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) in growing individuals. After skeletal maturity, the epiphyseal plate ossifies and the metaphysis merges with the diaphysis.

Anatomik ta'rif: An indentation or concavity on the edge of a bone. The sciatic notch of the pelvis (greater and lesser) transmits the sciatic nerve and other neurovascular structures; the trochlear notch of the ulna articulates with the humerus.

Anatomik ta'rif: The process of bone tissue formation. Intramembranous ossification forms flat bones directly from mesenchyme; endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model with bone, forming most of the axial and appendicular skeleton.

Anatomik ta'rif: A bone-forming cell derived from mesenchymal stem cells that synthesizes and secretes the organic matrix (osteoid) of bone and regulates its subsequent mineralization with calcium and phosphate. When surrounded by matrix, an osteoblast becomes an osteocyte.

Anatomik ta'rif: A large, multinucleated cell derived from hematopoietic monocyte precursors that resorbs bone by secreting hydrochloric acid and proteolytic enzymes into a resorption lacuna (Howship's lacuna). It is the principal cell responsible for bone remodeling and turnover.

Anatomik ta'rif: A mature bone cell enclosed within a lacuna (small cavity) in the bone matrix, connected to neighboring osteocytes and the periosteum via canaliculi (tiny channels) through which nutrients and signals are exchanged. Osteocytes are the most abundant bone cells and act as mechanosensors.

Anatomik ta'rif: The dense fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of bone except at articular cartilage. The outer fibrous layer provides attachment for tendons and ligaments; the inner osteogenic layer contains osteoblasts essential for bone growth and repair.

Anatomik ta'rif: Any prominent projection or outgrowth from a bone. Processes serve as attachment sites for muscles and ligaments. Examples include the styloid process of the temporal bone, the coracoid process of the scapula, and the transverse processes of vertebrae.

Anatomik ta'rif: A sharp, slender projection of bone, sharper than a tubercle or process. The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae; vertebral spinous processes are palpable along the back.

Anatomik ta'rif: A groove or furrow on the surface of a bone, often accommodating tendons, vessels, or nerves. The intertubercular sulcus (bicipital groove) of the humerus guides the long head of the biceps tendon.

Anatomik ta'rif: A fibrous immovable joint between adjacent bones of the skull. Major sutures include the coronal, sagittal, lambdoid, and squamous sutures. Premature fusion of sutures (craniosynostosis) can restrict brain growth.

Anatomik ta'rif: A large, blunt, irregular bony prominence found exclusively on the femur. The greater trochanter is the insertion of several hip abductor muscles; the lesser trochanter receives the iliopsoas tendon. Trochanters are important surgical and clinical landmarks.

Anatomik ta'rif: A large, rough, rounded projection on a bone that serves as an attachment site for tendons and muscles. The tibial tuberosity is the insertion of the patellar tendon (quadriceps femoris); the greater tuberosity of the humerus anchors the rotator cuff.

Anatomik ta'rif: Perforating canals that run perpendicular or oblique to the long axis of bone, connecting adjacent Haversian canals, the periosteum, and the endosteum, and conveying blood vessels and nerves. Also called perforating canals.

Anatomik ta'rif: A globular protein that polymerizes to form the thin filaments of the sarcomere. During muscle contraction, myosin cross-bridges bind to actin and pull the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere, shortening the muscle.

Anatomik ta'rif: The primary muscle responsible for producing a specific movement; also called the prime mover. For elbow flexion, the biceps brachii is the agonist. Agonist activity is coordinated with antagonist inhibition to produce smooth movement.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle that opposes or reverses the action of an agonist. During elbow flexion, the triceps brachii is the antagonist. Antagonists relax to allow movement and contract to decelerate or reverse it.

Anatomik ta'rif: A flat, sheet-like tendon that attaches a broad muscle to bone or to another muscle. The external abdominal oblique aponeurosis and the epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) of the scalp are prominent examples.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle whose fibers are arranged in concentric rings around an opening (sphincter). Contraction closes the aperture. Examples include the orbicularis oculi (eye), orbicularis oris (mouth), and various sphincters of the gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle contraction in which the muscle shortens while under tension, producing movement in the direction of the contracting force. The biceps brachii undergoes concentric contraction when lifting a weight toward the shoulder.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle in which a broad origin converges onto a narrow insertion, with muscle fibers oriented at varying angles (fan-shaped). The pectoralis major is the classic example; convergent architecture allows the muscle to exert forces from multiple directions.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens while under tension, decelerating a movement or controlling a load. Eccentric contractions generate the greatest forces and are the most common cause of delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).

Anatomik ta'rif: The delicate sheath of connective tissue surrounding each individual muscle fiber (cell). It contains capillaries and nerve terminals that supply the fiber and contributes to the tendon at the muscle's insertion.

Anatomik ta'rif: The outermost connective tissue sheath surrounding an entire skeletal muscle. The epimysium is continuous with the deep fascia and the tendons at both ends of the muscle, and it transmits contractile forces to the skeleton.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle that stabilizes the origin of an agonist by anchoring the proximal bone, allowing the agonist to exert its force more efficiently on the distal bone. The scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids) act as fixators during arm movements.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing a spindle-shaped muscle with fibers running parallel to the line of pull, tapering at each end into tendons. Fusiform muscles (e.g., biceps brachii) have greater range of contraction but lower force per unit volume compared with pennate muscles.

Anatomik ta'rif: A type of muscle contraction where the muscle generates tension without changing its length. Isometric contractions occur during postural holding and joint stabilization, such as maintaining a plank position.

Anatomik ta'rif: A type of muscle contraction where the muscle changes length while maintaining relatively constant tension. Isotonic contractions are subdivided into concentric (shortening) and eccentric (lengthening) contractions.

Anatomik ta'rif: The specialized region of skeletal muscle fiber membrane (sarcolemma) that forms one side of the neuromuscular junction, containing a high density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Binding of acetylcholine generates the end plate potential that triggers muscle contraction.

Anatomik ta'rif: A single motor neuron and all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates. All fibers of a motor unit contract together (all-or-none principle). Fine motor control (e.g., eye muscles) uses small units with few fibers; postural muscles use larger units.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cylindrical bundle of contractile proteins (actin and myosin) running the length of a muscle fiber. Each muscle cell (fiber) contains hundreds of parallel myofibrils, which in turn contain thousands of sarcomeres in series.

Anatomik ta'rif: The molecular motor protein forming the thick filaments of the sarcomere. Myosin heads hydrolyze ATP to generate the power stroke that moves actin filaments, producing force and shortening. It is the most abundant protein in muscle tissue.

Anatomik ta'rif: The chemical synapse between a motor neuron's axon terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber's motor end plate. Acetylcholine released into the synaptic cleft binds receptors to trigger an action potential and muscle contraction; it is the site of action of neuromuscular blocking agents and botulinum toxin.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing a muscle fiber arrangement in which fibers are oriented at an angle to the line of pull (like a feather — Latin: penna). Pennate muscles (unipennate, bipennate, multipennate) pack more fibers into a given volume, generating greater force than parallel-fiber muscles of the same size.

Anatomik ta'rif: A layer of connective tissue that bundles groups of muscle fibers into fascicles. The perimysium contains blood vessels and nerves that supply the fascicle and is thicker than the endomysium.

Anatomik ta'rif: The muscle primarily responsible for a specific action at a joint; synonymous with agonist. In shoulder abduction, the deltoid is the prime mover, while the supraspinatus initiates and assists the movement.

Anatomik ta'rif: A band of thickened deep fascia that holds tendons in place as they cross a joint, preventing bowstringing during movement. The flexor and extensor retinacula at the wrist and ankle are clinically important; carpal tunnel syndrome occurs within the flexor retinaculum.

Anatomik ta'rif: The basic contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber, bounded by two Z-discs. It contains overlapping thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments; sliding of these filaments past each other produces muscle shortening according to the sliding filament theory.

Anatomik ta'rif: A muscle that assists the agonist in performing a movement or that stabilizes a joint to make the agonist more effective. Synergists reduce unnecessary motion and increase the efficiency of the prime mover.

Anatomik ta'rif: A tiny, thin-walled air sac at the terminus of the bronchiolar tree where gas exchange occurs. The human lungs contain approximately 300-500 million alveoli, providing a total surface area of about 70 square meters for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.

Anatomik ta'rif: A small airway less than 1 mm in diameter that lacks cartilage in its walls, relying instead on smooth muscle to regulate airway diameter. Terminal bronchioles lead to respiratory bronchioles and ultimately to alveolar ducts; their smooth muscle is the target of bronchodilator therapy in asthma.

Anatomik ta'rif: A large cartilage-reinforced airway of the conducting zone. The trachea divides into the right and left main (primary) bronchi, which subdivide into lobar (secondary) and segmental (tertiary) bronchi supplying each bronchopulmonary segment.

Anatomik ta'rif: The volume of air that occupies the conducting airways and does not participate in gas exchange. Anatomical dead space (~150 mL) is the volume in the trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles; physiological dead space also includes non-perfused alveoli.

Anatomik ta'rif: The dome-shaped musculotendinous sheet separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It is the principal muscle of inspiration; when it contracts, it flattens and descends, increasing thoracic volume and drawing air into the lungs.

Anatomik ta'rif: The diffusion of oxygen from alveolar air into pulmonary capillary blood, and of carbon dioxide in the reverse direction, driven by partial pressure gradients. Efficient gas exchange depends on a thin alveolar-capillary membrane, adequate surface area, and matched ventilation and perfusion.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cartilaginous structure in the anterior neck (C3-C6) that connects the pharynx to the trachea. It houses the vocal folds (cords) for phonation, serves as the entrance to the lower airways, and contains the epiglottis, which prevents aspiration during swallowing.

Anatomik ta'rif: A fibromuscular tube behind the nasal and oral cavities that serves as a common passage for food and air. It is divided into the nasopharynx (posterior to the nasal cavity), oropharynx (posterior to the oral cavity), and laryngopharynx (hypopharynx).

Anatomik ta'rif: The serous membrane enveloping each lung. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface; the parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum. The two layers are continuous at the lung hilum.

Anatomik ta'rif: The potential space between the visceral and parietal pleural layers containing a small amount of serous fluid that reduces friction during breathing. A pneumothorax occurs when air enters this space, causing lung collapse.

Anatomik ta'rif: A complex mixture of phospholipids and proteins (primarily dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) secreted by Type II pneumocytes that reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Deficiency causes respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants.

Anatomik ta'rif: The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single normal, quiet breath, approximately 500 mL in a healthy adult. Tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate equals minute ventilation, a key measure of respiratory function.

Anatomik ta'rif: The cartilaginous and membranous tube extending from the larynx (at the level of C6) to the carina (at T4-T5) where it divides into the two main bronchi. It is supported by 16-20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings that prevent collapse.

Anatomik ta'rif: The mechanical process of moving air in and out of the lungs through the respiratory tract. Pulmonary ventilation is driven by pressure differences created by respiratory muscle activity and is distinct from gas exchange (respiration at the alveolar level).

Anatomik ta'rif: The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation, equal to the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume. It is approximately 4.5-5 L in a healthy adult and is reduced in restrictive lung diseases.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cluster of secretory cells (acinar cells) in the exocrine pancreas that produce and secrete digestive enzymes (including amylase, lipase, and proteases) into a central lumen that drains into the pancreatic duct system. Acinar cells are vulnerable to autodigestion in pancreatitis.

Anatomik ta'rif: A yellow-green alkaline fluid produced by hepatocytes and stored in the gallbladder. It contains bile salts, bilirubin, cholesterol, phospholipids, and electrolytes. Bile salts emulsify dietary fats in the small intestine to facilitate enzymatic digestion and absorption.

Anatomik ta'rif: The sac-like pouches of the large intestine formed by contraction of the taeniae coli, giving the colon its characteristic segmented appearance on imaging. Haustral contractions slowly mix colonic contents and absorb water.

Anatomik ta'rif: The basic structural and functional unit of the liver, roughly hexagonal in shape, consisting of hepatocytes arranged in plates radiating from a central vein, with portal triads (portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch, bile duct) at each corner. Blood flows from the portal triads inward to the central vein.

Anatomik ta'rif: Clusters of endocrine cells scattered throughout the exocrine pancreatic tissue, comprising approximately 1-2% of pancreatic volume. They contain alpha cells (glucagon), beta cells (insulin), delta cells (somatostatin), and PP cells, regulating blood glucose homeostasis.

Anatomik ta'rif: A double fold of peritoneum that attaches the small intestine to the posterior abdominal wall and carries the blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves supplying the gut. Once considered multiple separate structures, the mesentery is now recognized as a single continuous organ.

Anatomik ta'rif: Microscopic projections on the apical surface of enterocytes (intestinal absorptive cells) that form the brush border, further amplifying the absorptive surface by approximately 600-fold. They contain digestive enzymes including lactase, sucrase, and maltase.

Anatomik ta'rif: An apron-like fold of peritoneum attached to the stomach and transverse colon. The greater omentum drapes over the abdominal organs and contains fat; the lesser omentum connects the stomach and duodenum to the liver. The omentum limits the spread of intraperitoneal infection.

Anatomik ta'rif: Coordinated, sequential smooth muscle contractions and relaxations that propel ingested material along the gastrointestinal tract. It is initiated by the enteric nervous system and can occur independently of the central nervous system.

Anatomik ta'rif: The serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering most of the abdominal organs. The parietal peritoneum lines the cavity wall; the visceral peritoneum covers organs. The peritoneal cavity normally contains only a small amount of lubricating fluid.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing organs located behind the parietal peritoneum in the retroperitoneal space. Primary retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, adrenal glands, aorta, IVC) were never suspended by mesentery; secondary retroperitoneal organs (duodenum, pancreas, ascending/descending colon) became retroperitoneal during embryonic development.

Anatomik ta'rif: Large longitudinal folds in the mucosa of the stomach that allow the organ to distend when filled with food. Rugae are most prominent in the empty stomach and flatten as the stomach fills, increasing capacity to approximately 1-1.5 L.

Anatomik ta'rif: A ring of smooth or skeletal muscle that controls the passage of material through a tubular structure. Key GI sphincters include the lower esophageal sphincter (preventing reflux), pyloric sphincter (regulating gastric emptying), and internal/external anal sphincters.

Anatomik ta'rif: Three distinct longitudinal bands of the outer smooth muscle layer that run along the length of the large intestine (except the rectum and appendix). Their continuous tonic contraction gathers the colon into haustra. The three taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a surgical landmark.

Anatomik ta'rif: Finger-like projections of the small intestinal mucosa (approximately 0.5-1.6 mm tall) that dramatically increase the absorptive surface area of the intestine. Each villus contains a central lacteal for fat absorption and a capillary network for nutrient absorption.

Anatomik ta'rif: The outer region of the adrenal gland, divided into three zones: zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids, primarily cortisol), and zona reticularis (androgens). It is derived from mesoderm.

Anatomik ta'rif: The inner region of the adrenal gland, composed of chromaffin cells derived from neural crest. It secretes catecholamines (primarily epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to sympathetic stimulation, mediating the 'fight-or-flight' response.

Anatomik ta'rif: The primary reproductive endocrine organs: testes in males and ovaries in females. Gonads produce steroid sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen, progesterone) under pituitary FSH and LH control, and produce gametes (sperm and ova).

Anatomik ta'rif: A chemical messenger secreted by endocrine cells into the bloodstream that exerts regulatory effects on distant target cells bearing specific receptors. Hormones are classified as amino acid-derived, peptide/protein, or steroid, each with distinct mechanisms of action.

Anatomik ta'rif: The diencephalic region that integrates the nervous and endocrine systems by producing releasing and inhibiting hormones that control anterior pituitary secretion, and by synthesizing oxytocin and ADH for posterior pituitary release. It is the supreme regulator of the endocrine system.

Anatomik ta'rif: A regulatory mechanism in which the output of a physiological system inhibits its own production, maintaining homeostasis. The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis is a classic example: high thyroid hormone levels suppress TSH and TRH secretion.

Anatomik ta'rif: The endocrine component of the pancreas (Islets of Langerhans) that regulates blood glucose homeostasis. Beta cells secrete insulin (lowering blood glucose); alpha cells secrete glucagon (raising blood glucose); delta cells secrete somatostatin (inhibiting both).

Anatomik ta'rif: Four small glands embedded on the posterior surface of the thyroid that secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), the principal regulator of calcium and phosphate homeostasis. PTH raises blood calcium by stimulating bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and renal activation of vitamin D.

Anatomik ta'rif: A small pine cone-shaped endocrine gland in the epithalamus that produces melatonin, a hormone regulating circadian rhythms and the sleep-wake cycle. Melatonin secretion is inhibited by light and peaks during darkness.

Anatomik ta'rif: A pea-sized endocrine gland suspended from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum and housed in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone. The anterior pituitary secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, and prolactin; the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH (vasopressin).

Anatomik ta'rif: A regulatory mechanism in which the output of a system amplifies further production, driving the system away from equilibrium until a threshold is reached. The pre-ovulatory LH surge driven by rising estrogen is a key endocrine example; oxytocin during childbirth is another.

Anatomik ta'rif: A protein on or within a target cell that binds a specific hormone or signaling molecule and initiates a biological response. Cell-surface receptors (for peptide hormones) use second messengers; intracellular receptors (for steroid hormones) directly regulate gene transcription.

Anatomik ta'rif: A cell that possesses specific receptors for a particular hormone and responds to it. Specificity of endocrine signaling depends on receptor expression rather than hormone distribution, as hormones circulate throughout the body but affect only cells with appropriate receptors.

Anatomik ta'rif: A bilobed lymphoid and endocrine organ in the anterior mediastinum that is most active in childhood and involutes after puberty. It is essential for T-lymphocyte maturation and secretes thymosin hormones that promote T-cell differentiation.

Anatomik ta'rif: A bilobed endocrine gland in the anterior neck that produces thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) regulating metabolic rate, growth, and development, and calcitonin regulating calcium homeostasis. It is the largest pure endocrine gland in the body.

Anatomik ta'rif: A specialized loose connective tissue composed predominantly of lipid-filled adipocytes. White adipose tissue stores energy, cushions organs, and provides thermal insulation; brown adipose tissue (more prominent in infants) generates heat via non-shivering thermogenesis.

Anatomik ta'rif: A loose connective tissue with a loosely woven mesh of collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers embedded in abundant ground substance, containing fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells. It is the most widely distributed connective tissue, forming the packaging material of the body.

Anatomik ta'rif: A specialized fluid connective tissue consisting of formed elements (erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets) suspended in a liquid extracellular matrix (plasma). Blood transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products and mediates immune and hemostatic responses.

Anatomik ta'rif: A specialized connective tissue with a mineralized extracellular matrix of hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate crystals) embedded in an organic collagen framework, giving it exceptional compressive and tensile strength. Bone tissue is organized as compact (cortical) or spongy (cancellous) bone.

Anatomik ta'rif: A rigid but flexible avascular connective tissue composed of chondrocytes embedded in an extracellular matrix of collagen and proteoglycans (primarily aggrecan). It covers articular surfaces, forms the growth plates, and provides structural support in the ear and nose.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing epithelial cells that are taller than they are wide, with an oval nucleus typically located in the basal region. Simple columnar epithelium lines most of the GI tract and is specialized for absorption; pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract.

Anatomik ta'rif: The most abundant and widely distributed of the four primary tissue types, characterized by cells embedded in a large extracellular matrix of fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) and ground substance. It supports, connects, and protects other tissues and organs.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing epithelial cells that are approximately equal in height and width (cube-shaped), with a centrally placed nucleus. Simple cuboidal epithelium lines kidney tubules and small gland ducts where it specializes in secretion and absorption.

Anatomik ta'rif: A type of dense connective tissue in which collagen fibers are randomly interwoven in multiple planes, providing strength in all directions. It forms the dermis of the skin, joint capsules, and the fibrous periosteum.

Anatomik ta'rif: A type of dense connective tissue in which collagen fibers are arranged in parallel bundles, giving high tensile strength in one direction. Tendons and ligaments are composed of dense regular connective tissue.

Anatomik ta'rif: A flexible cartilage containing abundant elastic fibers in addition to type II collagen, giving it resilience and the ability to withstand repeated bending. Found in the auricle (outer ear), epiglottis, and Eustachian tube.

Anatomik ta'rif: A specialized connective tissue rich in elastin fibers that allows structures to stretch and recoil. Found in the walls of large arteries (allowing them to dampen pulsatile blood flow), the trachea, and the ligamentum flavum of the vertebral column.

Anatomik ta'rif: One of the four primary tissue types, consisting of tightly packed cells with little extracellular matrix that cover body surfaces, line body cavities, and form glands. Epithelium is avascular and is classified by cell shape and number of layers.

Anatomik ta'rif: A tough cartilage containing abundant type I collagen bundles in addition to type II collagen and proteoglycans, combining the tensile strength of dense connective tissue with the compressive resistance of cartilage. Found in intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and menisci.

Anatomik ta'rif: The most common type of cartilage, with a glassy, homogeneous matrix rich in type II collagen and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans. It covers articular surfaces (articular cartilage), forms the costal cartilages, the tracheal rings, and the fetal skeleton template.

Anatomik ta'rif: A loose connective tissue composed of a network of reticular fibers (fine type III collagen) secreted by reticular cells, forming the supportive stroma of lymphoid organs, bone marrow, the liver, and the spleen.

Anatomik ta'rif: An epithelium consisting of a single layer of cells, all in contact with the basement membrane. It is adapted for absorption and secretion in areas where mechanical stress is low, such as the intestinal lining and kidney tubules.

Anatomik ta'rif: Describing flat, scale-like epithelial cells. Simple squamous epithelium lines blood vessels (endothelium), body cavities (mesothelium), and the alveoli. Stratified squamous epithelium covers skin, oral mucosa, and the esophagus.

Anatomik ta'rif: An epithelium consisting of multiple cell layers, with only the basal layer contacting the basement membrane. It is found in areas subject to mechanical stress such as the skin (stratified squamous keratinized) and the oral mucosa.

Anatomik ta'rif: A stratified epithelium unique to the urinary tract (renal pelvis, ureters, bladder) that can stretch and change shape as the organ fills and empties. Also called urothelium, its surface cells (umbrella cells) are large and dome-shaped when relaxed.

Anatomik ta'rif: A thin extraembryonic membrane of ectodermal and mesodermal origin that encloses the embryo and fetus in a fluid-filled amniotic cavity. Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus, prevents adhesions, and allows fetal movement. Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) and polyhydramnios (too much) have clinical significance.

Anatomik ta'rif: The stage of human embryonic development (approximately day 5-6) consisting of a hollow sphere: an outer cell mass (trophoblast) that will form the placenta and extraembryonic membranes, and an inner cell mass (embryoblast) that will form the embryo proper. Implantation of the blastocyst into the uterine endometrium occurs around day 6-10.

Anatomik ta'rif: The outermost of the three primary germ layers of the embryo, formed during gastrulation. It gives rise to the epidermis and its derivatives (hair, nails, sweat glands), the nervous system (via neurulation), and the special sense organs.

Anatomik ta'rif: The innermost of the three primary germ layers. It gives rise to the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract, the respiratory tract, the urinary bladder, and the parenchyma of organs such as the liver, pancreas, and thyroid gland.

Anatomik ta'rif: The fundamental embryonic process (occurring during week 3 in humans) by which the bilaminar embryonic disc is converted into a trilaminar disc through formation of the primitive streak and migration of epiblast cells to form mesoderm and endoderm. It establishes the three primary germ layers.

Anatomik ta'rif: The middle of the three primary germ layers, situated between ectoderm and endoderm. It gives rise to muscle, bone, cartilage, connective tissue, the cardiovascular system, the kidneys, and the gonads.

Anatomik ta'rif: A transient population of multipotent cells arising at the lateral margins of the neural plate that migrate extensively and give rise to a diverse array of structures including peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes, adrenal medullary cells, craniofacial bones and cartilage, and cardiac outflow tract structures.

Anatomik ta'rif: The embryonic precursor to the central nervous system, formed when the flat neural plate of ectoderm rolls up and closes during neurulation (weeks 3-4 of development). The cranial portion forms the brain; the caudal portion forms the spinal cord. Failure to close causes neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

Anatomik ta'rif: The process (weeks 3-4) by which the neural plate, induced by the notochord, folds to form the neural tube. Cranial portions close first; failure at specific closure sites produces neural tube defects. Adequate maternal folate is essential for neural tube closure.

Anatomik ta'rif: A rod-like structure of mesodermal origin that forms the primitive axial skeleton of the embryo and defines the body axis. It induces formation of the neural plate (and ultimately the neural tube) and persists in adults as the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.

Anatomik ta'rif: The embryonic period (weeks 3-8) during which the major organ systems are established from the three germ layers. This is the period of greatest susceptibility to teratogens, as disruption at critical windows can cause major structural malformations.

Anatomik ta'rif: One of a series of mesodermal and neural crest-derived paired structures in the embryonic head and neck region (also called branchial arches), each containing a cartilaginous bar, a cranial nerve, and an aortic arch artery. They give rise to the bones, muscles, and vasculature of the face, jaw, and neck.

Anatomik ta'rif: The discoid organ formed by the interlocking of the fetal chorion (trophoblast-derived) and the maternal decidua basalis (endometrium) that facilitates the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste products between the fetal and maternal circulations without direct mixing of blood. It also produces hormones including hCG, progesterone, and estrogen.

Anatomik ta'rif: Paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm that form in a cranial-to-caudal sequence during embryonic development. Each somite differentiates into a sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), myotome (skeletal muscles of the trunk and limbs), and dermatome (dermis of the dorsal skin).

Anatomik ta'rif: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst that invades the uterine endometrium during implantation and differentiates into the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. It forms the fetal component of the placenta and produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.
Shifokor farmatsevtga (dorixonaga) ushbu dori vositasini berishni buyuruvchi asosiy so'z. Barcha retseptlar shu so'z bilan boshlanadi.
Retseptda dorining bir martalik dozasi yozilgandan so'ng, bemorga undan necha dona yoki ampula berish kerakligini ko'rsatuvchi qisqartma (Da tales doses numero).
Dorini qanday tartibda, qachon va qancha miqdorda ichish yoki qabul qilish kerakligi bemor tushunadigan tilda ko'rsatiladigan qism.
Dorixonada tayyorlanadigan dorilar uchun ko'rsatma (Misce, fiat). Masalan, kukun, malham yoki eritma tayyorlash buyrug'i.
Dori vositasining qattiq tabletka shaklida chiqarilgani va berilishi kerakligini bildiradi (in tabulettis).
Suyuq dori shakli. Tomirga, mushakka yuborish yoki ichish uchun mo'ljallangan suyultirilgan dori.
Steril shisha ampulada saqlanadigan, ineksiya (ukol) uchun mo'ljallangan dori shakli.
Ichida kukun yoki suyuq modda bo'lgan, oshqozon yoki ichakda eruvchan qobiqli dori shakli.
Suyuqlik ichida to'liq erimagan mayda dori zarralari bo'lgan suyuqlik. Ichishdan oldin chayqatiladi.
Teri yoki shilliq qavatlarga surtish uchun mo'ljallangan quyuq yog'simon dori shakli.
Ko'z, quloq, burun yoki ichish uchun mo'ljallangan tomchi holidagi dori shakli.
Dorini yutish, og'iz orqali ichish kerakligini ko'rsatuvchi eng ko'p uchraydigan qabul qilish usuli.
Dorini yutmasdan, til ostiga qo'yib so'rish kerakligini bildiradi (masalan, Validol yoki Glitserin).
Shamcha (svecha) yoki klizma vositalarini to'g'ri ichakka qo'llash usuli.
Ukolni mushak to'qimasiga (odatda dumba yoki yelka sohasiga) yuborish ko'rsatmasi.
Dorini bevosita qon tomiriga (venaga ukol yoki kapelnitsa orqali) quyish ko'rsatmasi.
Ukolni teri osti yog' qatlamiga yuborish (masalan, insulin preparatlari).
Kerakli konsistensiya yoki hajm hosil bo'lishi uchun kerakcha qo'shilsin degan ma'noda ishlatiladi.
Dorini ovqatlanishdan 20-30 daqiqa oldin ichish kerakligini anglatuvchi qisqartma.
Dorini ovqatlangandan so'ng qabul qilish kerakligini ko'rsatadi.
Shifokor dorixonaga ushbu dori zudlik bilan navbatsiz tayyorlanishi va berilishi kerakligini bildiruvchi belgi.
O'ta shoshilinch holatlarda dorini birinchi navbatda berish haqidagi buyruq.
Farmatsevtga dorini chiqarib berishni buyuruvchi lotincha fe'l.
Dorivor o'simlik yoki xomashyodan olingan quyuq yoki suyuq konsentrlangan modda.
Odatda spirtda tayyorlangan dorivor o'simlik damlamasi.
Maydalangan quruq dori moddasi.
Ko'pincha bolalar uchun tayyorlanadigan shirin quyuq suyuq dori shakli.
Tana haroratida eriydigan, to'g'ri ichakka yoki qinga qo'yiladigan dori vositasi.
Bir-birida erimaydigan ikki suyuqlik (masalan, yog' va suv) aralashmasi.
Tuzlar va aralashmalardan tozalangan, dori tayyorlashda ishlatiladigan maxsus suv.
Dorini bir kunda faqat bir mahal ichish kerakligi ko'rsatmasi.
Dorini sutkada 2 mahal (ertalab va kechqurun) qabul qilish tartibi.
Dorini kuniga 3 mahal qabul qilish kerakligini anglatuvchi ko'rsatma.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): The command center of the nervous system, the brain processes sensory information, controls motor function, regulates homeostasis, and generates consciousness, thought, memory, emotion, and language. It is the largest part of the central nervous system, weighing approximately 1.4 kilograms in adults, and comprises the cerebrum with its two hemispheres and frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, the cerebellum, and the brainstem, formed by the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. Stroke, or cerebrovascular accident, is a leading cause of disability, and traumatic brain injury ranges from concussion to severe diffuse axonal injury. Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 10, or BA10, is part of the frontal cortex in the human brain. BA10 encompasses the most anterior part of the frontal cortex, known as the frontopolar region. This area is believed to play a part in strategic processes involved in memory retrieval and executive function. This area is also called frontopolar area 10, and it refers to a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined frontal region of cerebral cortex. It occupies the most rostral portions of the superior frontal gyrus and the middle frontal gyrus. In humans, on the medial aspect of the hemisphere it is bounded ventrally by the superior rostral sulcus (H). It does not extend as far as the cingulate sulcus. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded dorsally by the granular frontal area 9, caudally by the middle frontal area 46, and ventrally by the orbital area 47 and by the rostral area 12 or, in an early version of Brodmann's cortical map (Brodmann-1909), the prefrontal Brodmann area 11-1909.
Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 11 is one of Brodmann's cytologically defined regions of the brain. It is involved in planning, reasoning, and decision making.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 12 is a subdivision of the cerebral cortex of the guenon defined on the basis of cytoarchitecture. It occupies the most rostral portion of the frontal lobe. Brodmann-1909 did not regard it as homologous, either topographically or cytoarchitecturally, to rostral area 12 of the human. Distinctive features (Brodmann-1905): a quite distinct internal granular layer (IV) separates slender pyramidal cells of the external pyramidal layer (III) and the internal pyramidal layer (V); the multiform layer (VI) is expanded, contains widely dispersed spindle cells and merges gradually with the underlying cortical white matter; all cells, including the pyramidal cells of the external and internal pyramidal layers are inordinately small; the internal pyramidal layer (V) also contains spindle cells in groups of two to five located close to its border with the internal granular layer (IV).

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 13 is a subdivision of the cerebral cortex as defined on the guenon monkey and on the basis of cytoarchitecture. Brodmann area 13 is found in humans, however it seems to act as a bridge between the lateral and medial layers of the brain. Thus it is sometimes misidentified as not being a Brodmann area.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann Area 14 is one of Brodmann's subdivisions of the cerebral cortex in the brain. It was defined by Brodmann in the guenon monkey. No equivalent structure exists in humans.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann Area 15 is one of Brodmann's subdivisions of the cerebral cortex in the brain. Area 15 was defined by Brodmann in the guenon monkey, but he found no equivalent structure in humans. However, functional imaging experiments have found structures that may be homologous.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 16 is a subdivision of the cerebral cortex of the guenon defined on the basis of cytoarchitecture. It is a relatively undifferentiated cortical area that Brodmann regarded as part of the insula because of the relation of its innermost multiform layer (VI) with the claustrum (VICl). The laminar organization of cortex is almost totally lacking. The molecular layer (I) is wide as in area 15 of Brodmann-1905. The space between layer I and layer VI is composed of a mixture of pyramidal cells and spindle cells with no significant number of granule cells. Pyramidal cells clump in the outer part to form glomeruli similar to those seen in some of the primary olfactory areas (Brodmann-1905). This term also refers to an area known as peripaleocortical claustral - a cytoarchitecturally defined (agranular) portion of the insula at its rostral extreme where it approaches most closely the claustrum and the prepyriform area (Stephan-76).

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): A subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined occipital region of cerebral cortex in the human. Defined by the band of Gennari, which gives it the name striate (furrowed) area, it occupies the banks of the calcarine sulcus which are located in the cuneus and the lingual gyrus of the occipital lobe. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded by the area 18 of Brodmann (human) which surrounds it ( Brodmann-1909 ). In the mouse ( Paxinos-2001 ) and the rat ( Swanson-1998 ) it is located on the dorsolateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere[BrainInfo].
Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): The Latin name for the Brodmann (1909) area 18 is area 18 of Brodmann.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 19, or BA19, is part of the occipital lobe cortex in the human brain. Along with area 18, it comprises the extrastriate (or peristriate) cortex. In normally-sighted humans, extrastriate cortex is a visual association area, with feature-extracting, shape recognition, attentional, and multimodal integrating functions. This area is also known as peristriate area 19, and it refers to a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined occipital region of cerebral cortex. In the human it is located in parts of the lingual gyrus, the cuneus, the lateral occipital gyrus (H) and the superior occipital gyrus (H) of the occipital lobe where it is bounded approximately by the parieto-occipital sulcus. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded on one side by the parastriate area 18 which it surrounds. Rostrally it is bounded by the angular area 39 (H) and the occipitotemporal area 37 (H) (Brodmann-1909).
Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): A region of the brain (Brodmann (1909) area 2) that contributes to neural processing within its functional domain.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 20, or BA20, is part of the temporal cortex in the human brain. The region encompasses most of the ventral temporal cortex, a region believed to play a part in high-level visual processing and recognition memory. This area is also known as inferior temporal area 20, and it refers to a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined temporal region of cerebral cortex. In the human it corresponds approximately to the inferior temporal gyrus. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded medially by the ectorhinal area 36 (H), laterally by the middle temporal area 21, rostrally by the temporopolar area 38 (H) and caudally by the occipitotemporal area 37 (H) (Brodmann-1909).

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 21, or BA21, is part of the temporal cortex in the human brain. The region encompasses most of the lateral temporal cortex, a region believed to play a part in auditory processing and language. Language function is left lateralized in most individuals. BA21 is superior to BA20 and inferior to BA40 and BA41. This area is also known as middle temporal area 21. It is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined temporal region of cerebral cortex. In the human it corresponds approximately to the middle temporal gyrus. It is bounded rostrally by the temporopolar area 38 (H), ventrally by the inferior temporal area 20, caudally by the occipitotemporal area 37 (H), and dorsally by the superior temporal area 22 (Brodmann-1909). [WP,unvetted].
Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 22 is one of Brodmann's cytologically defined regions of the brain. It is involved in auditory processing.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 25 (BA25) is an area in the cerebral cortex of the brain and delineated based on its cytoarchitectonic characteristics. The posterior parolfactory sulcus separates the paraterminal gyrus from BA25. Rostrally it is bound by the prefrontal area 11 of Brodmann.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 31, also known as dorsal posterior cingulate area 31, is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined cingulate region of the cerebral cortex. In the human it occupies portions of the posterior cingulate gyrus and medial aspect of the parietal lobe. Approximate boundaries are the cingulate sulcus dorsally and the parieto-occipital sulcus caudally. It partially surrounds the subparietal sulcus, the ventral continuation of the cingulate sulcus in the parietal lobe. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded rostrally by the ventral anterior cingulate area 24, ventrally by the ventral posterior cingulate area 23, dorsally by the gigantopyramidal area 4 and preparietal area 5 and caudally by the superior parietal area 7 (H) (Brodmann-1909).

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): The Brodmann area 32, also known in the human brain as the dorsal anterior cingulate area 32, refers to a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined cingulate region of cerebral cortex. In the human it forms an outer arc around the anterior cingulate gyrus. The cingulate sulcus defines approximately its inner boundary and the superior rostral sulcus (H) its ventral boundary; rostrally it extends almost to the margin of the frontal lobe. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded internally by the ventral anterior cingulate area 24, externally by medial margins of the agranular frontal area 6, intermediate frontal area 8, granular frontal area 9, frontopolar area 10, and prefrontal area 11-1909. (Brodmann19-09). Dorsal region of anterior cingulate gyrus is associated with rational thought processes, most notably active during the Stroop task.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 33, also known as pregenual area 33, is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined cingulate region of cerebral cortex. It is a narrow band located in the anterior cingulate gyrus adjacent to the supracallosal gyrus in the depth of the callosal sulcus, near the genu of the corpus callosum. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded by the ventral anterior cingulate area 24 and the supracallosal gyrus (Brodmann-1909).
Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 35, together with Brodmann area 36, is most frequently referred to as perirhinal cortex.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Ectorhinal area 36 is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined temporal region of cerebral cortex. With its medial boundary corresponding approximately to the rhinal sulcus it is located primarily in the fusiform gyrus. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded laterally and caudally by the inferior temporal area 20, medially by the perirhinal area 35 and rostrally by the temporopolar area 38 (H) (Brodmann-1909). Together with Brodmann area 35, it comprises the perirhinal cortex.

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 37, or BA37, is part of the temporal cortex in the human brain. This area is known as occipitotemporal area 37 (H). It is a subdivision of the cytoarchitecturally defined temporal region of cerebral cortex. It is located primarily in the caudal portions of the fusiform gyrus and inferior temporal gyrus on the mediobasal and lateral surfaces at the caudal extreme of the temporal lobe. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded caudally by the peristriate Brodmann area 19, rostrally by the inferior temporal area 20 and middle temporal area 21 and dorsally on the lateral aspect of the hemisphere by the angular area 39 (H) (Brodmann-1909).

Anatomik ta'rif (Ichki a'zo): Brodmann area 40, or BA40, is part of the parietal cortex in the human brain. The inferior part of BA40 is in the area of the supramarginal gyrus, which lies at the posterior end of the lateral fissure, in the inferior lateral part of the parietal lobe. It is bounded approximately by the intraparietal sulcus, the inferior postcentral sulcus, the posterior subcentral sulcus and the lateral sulcus. Cytoarchitecturally it is bounded caudally by the angular area 39 (H), rostrally and dorsally by the caudal postcentral area 2, and ventrally by the subcentral area 43 and the superior temporal area 22 (Brodmann-1909). Cytoarchitectonically defined subregions of rostral BA40/the supramarginal gyrus are PF, PFcm, PFm, PFop, and PFt. Area PF is the homologue to macaque area PF, part of the mirror neuron system, and active in humans during imitation. The supramarginal gyrus part of Brodmann area 40 is the region in the inferior parietal lobe that is involved in reading both in regards to meaning and phonology. [WP,unvetted].
